newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First Party says election about who owns NZ.
newsitem.headline: NZ First Party says election about who owns NZ.

text.p: The opposition New Zealand First Party launched its campaign on Monday for a general election which leader Winston Peters said would be about "who owns New Zealand".

"We are not a party that sells this country off to foreigners and rich corporates," Peters told the campaign launch in Auckland in a speech dominated by attacks on the conservative National Party government and big business.
The populist leader also renewed attacks on the central bank's monetary policy, saying the high New Zealand dollar was "killing" exporters.

He catalogued the "roll of shame" of NZ$16 billion in asset sales by the National government and its Labour predecessor. Peters said a National government would continue the sales and make New Zealanders "virtual peasants in our own land".
He promised a society "that does not kowtow to rich tax- concealing corporates or to foreigners who want to own our country".
New Zealand First is running on a platform to preserve the country's economic sovereignty. Latest opinion polls show it in second place behind National with 19 percent support.
Labour, New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance are jointly polling just above 50 percent in the run-up to the October 12 election, New Zealand's first under proportional representation.
Replying to criticism from the Alliance that he was planning to do a deal with National after the election, Peters said his was "the only opposition party that can bust National".
Almost half his speech was devoted to criticising National and its allies, with only passing sideswipes at the other main opposition parties.

National launched its campaign in Auckland on Sunday with Prime Minister Jim Bolger warning of the threat to the economy of the three opposition parties -- what he called "the gloom gang" of New Zealand First, Labour and the left-wing Alliance.

Peters countered on Monday calling National and its likely coalition partners, free-market ACT and the Christian Coalition, "the toxic trio". He said all three elements of this "far right, three-headed monster" were funded by big business.
"New Zealand First is not for the rich corporates who hide their tax millions in the Cook Islands and rob the New Zealand people blind and expect knighthoods at home," Peters said.
A commission of inquiry, set up in 1994 in response to allegations by Peters, is investigating use of the Cooks Islands as a tax haven by New Zealand corporates in the 1980s.
Peters said New Zealand First had the policies to fix high interest rates and a sagging economy.

Projections released last week showed Treasury expected growth to slow to 2.5 percent in the year to March 1997 before accelerating to 3.7 percent in 1998. But Reserve Bank projections were for growth of 2.0 percent and 2.4 percent.
Peters said all recent economic indicators pointed to an economy in decline.
"Our economic and export policies abandon National's obsession with monetary policy, with high interest rates and a kiwi dollar that is killing our exporters," Peters said.
New Zealand First wants to change the current Reserve Bank target of 0-2 percent inflation to a broader one which aims for inflation below that of New Zealand's top 10 trading partners.
